newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemala's U.S. military attache called home.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala's U.S. military attache called home.

text.p: Guatemala's military attache in Washington, Gen. Roberto Letona, has been ordered home after he was linked to a top figure in a corruption scandal, an army spokesman said on Monday.

"Under instructions from the president, Letona was removed from his military post," Capt. Victor Ramiro Roulet of the Army Information Department told Reuters. He said Letona would continue to receive a salary and be assigned to the army's general barracks in Guatemala City while the army conducted an internal investigation.
Col. Cesar Ruis Morales, director of civil affairs for national defence, will become the new military attache.

Letona was the latest casualty in an unprecedented purge of suspected corrupt officials and army officers that began in September with the arrest of alleged crime boss Alfredo Moreno, a former army intelligence employee.

Prosecutors say Moreno ran an enormous smuggling operation that cheated the government out of an estimated $2.7 billion in taxes and duties over 15 years. Military, customs and national guard members apparently working for Moreno ensured that a constant stream of trucks loaded with merchandise entered the country without paying duties or taxes.

The government began to look into Letona's links with Moreno after local newspapers published photographs of the two men together. Letona is the second general to lose his job in the scandal after Gen. Cesar Augusto Garcia Gonzalez, deputy defence minister, who was fired on Sept. 17.

Another deputy minister, Mario Rene Cifuentes of the Interior Ministry, was fired on Sept. 30 after photographs linked him to Moreno. Also dismissed in the past two months were more than 40 government employees linked to Moreno including regional police chiefs, customs administrators and a judge.

Moreno, who is in a Guatemala City jail, has been the only person arrested in the case. But courts have frozen bank accounts of suspects and have issued orders preventing people under investigation from leaving the country.

President Alvaro Arzu, in office since January, has won high praise from diplomats for his strong attack on corruption and for daring to take on the powerful army, which rights groups say is notorious for protecting its interests through threats and assassinations.
